newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Senate to debate Telstra, labour law.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Senate to debate Telstra, labour law.

text.p: Bills for the Australian government's labour reform and proposed partial sale of telecoms carrier Telstra Corp may both go to a vote in the upper house of parliament next week, a government spokeswoman said on Friday.
With these two priority bills through the parliamentary process, the way will then become clear for the movement of the government's remaining budget measures.

A draft programme for the upper house, the Senate, lists the government's Workplace Relations bill for final debate on Monday, while the Telstra bill is scheduled to be dealt with on Wednesday and Thursday.
However, the programme is usually optimistic.
The Workplace Relations bill has passed initial formalities in the Senate and is now in the upper house's amendment process.
However, it is expected to be passed because the Australian Democrats have agreed to back the bill with certain amendments.
The government needs two extra votes to pass any legislation in the Senate, where it does not have a majority.
"Definitely industrial relations (will be finished next week)," a spokeswoman for government leader in the Senate, Robert Hill, told Reuters.
The bill would deregulate the Australian labour market and give unions a weaker role in wage negotiations.
The Telstra bill is still to be voted on in the Senate at the initial stage, and then has to go to the committee stage where it would be amended.
Amendments are expected but neither the government nor the bill's opponents are sure whether it will pass at all.

The Democrats and the Labor opposition are both opposed to the proposed sale of one-third of Telstra, leaving Independents Brian Harradine and Mal Colston as the only possible source of the two extra votes that the government must have.
A Greens spokesman said Harradine and Colston are widely expected to vote for the bill initially but may not back it in the final vote, following all amendments.
The government expects to raise about A$8.0 billion through the sale.
